architectural_implications.after: A fast typed model returns Choice/Score/Noul answers at the decision points, while a generative model is invoked only when text is actually required.
architectural_implications.before: A single LLM prompt handles classification, routing, and tool selection alongside text generation, with all outputs parsed from prose.
architectural_implications.consequence: Harness code becomes the orchestrator of heterogeneous models; interface definitions and thresholds, not prompts, become the primary artifacts to maintain.
architectural_implications.observation: Decision-making is factored out of the generative model into a separate, typed-answer service callable from middleware.

architectural_implications.after: Middleware evaluates risk with a typed decision and can block the call outright before the tool runs.
architectural_implications.before: Guardrails are expressed as system-prompt instructions and hope the model complies before calling a destructive tool.
architectural_implications.consequence: Irreversible operations gain a deterministic choke point, but the harness owner now owns that gate's correctness and false-block behavior.
architectural_implications.observation: Safety checks move into a pre-execution interception layer between agent intent and side effect.

architectural_implications.after: A router decision assigns each request to a fast or deep model based on task requirements.
architectural_implications.before: A single model (or hand-tuned per-feature selection) serves all traffic, so simple and complex tasks pay the same cost and latency.
architectural_implications.consequence: Cost and latency profile becomes tunable at runtime, with new failure modes around misrouting and router overhead.
architectural_implications.observation: Routing between cheap and expensive models becomes a runtime function of the prompt rather than a static choice.

article_ideas.angle: Trace a single tool-call round trip and separate the bytes that exist for the machine from the bytes that exist for a human reader; show what disappears when the machine-facing layer returns typed decisions instead of prose.
article_ideas.audience: Agent and backend engineers designing internal agent interfaces
article_ideas.based_on: Traditional tool calling uses text generation as a bridge between machine execution and human interfaces, which is inefficient.
article_ideas.thesis: Using text generation as the bridge between machine execution and human interfaces couples backend agent logic to a human-readable format it never needed, and the fix is to make every internal decision boundary carry typed data, reserving prose for the boundaries where a human actually reads the output.
article_ideas.title: Your Agent's Control Flow Should Not Speak English

article_ideas.angle: Argue that any irreversible tool warrants an interception point between model intent and side effect, then enumerate the new obligations the harness owner inherits once that gate exists.
article_ideas.based_on: Jev middleware can intercept tool calls and block destructive actions based on defined safety criteria.
article_ideas.thesis: Tool-call safety expressed as system-prompt instructions is a probabilistic suggestion, while a pre-execution interception layer is a deterministic choke point; moving authorization into the call path changes who is accountable for irreversible actions and makes false-block behavior an explicit engineering concern rather than an emergent one.
article_ideas.title: The Harness Owns the Gate, Not the Prompt

article_ideas.angle: Treat routing as a heterogeneous-fleet problem: every mixed cheap/expensive fleet needs an explicit, logged routing decision, and the router's misroute rate is the metric that determines whether the fleet is worth having.
article_ideas.based_on: Model router middleware uses Jev to select between fast and deep models based on prompt complexity.
article_ideas.thesis: Model routing is itself a decision, so the component that arbitrates between cheap and expensive models should be the cheapest and most auditable part of the runtime; a router that costs as much as the thing it routes is a net negative and should be replaced by static configuration.
article_ideas.title: The Cheapest Model in the Stack Should Be the Router

article_ideas.angle: Take the headline multipliers seriously as a claim and list the measurement conditions that would need to hold for them to survive contact with a production workload.
article_ideas.based_on: Jev is 200-200x faster and 40-400x cheaper than traditional LLMs for structured choices.
article_ideas.thesis: Comparative performance claims about decision models are only actionable when stated with a task set, a baseline, and a volume assumption; until then they should be treated as a hypothesis to test rather than a budget line, because the cost profile at production volumes can invert the ranking.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Sydney Runkle, Allie Laabs, Hunter Lovell
  • Channel: LangChain
  • Main topic: Building an agent harness using Jev and LangChain with TypeSafe
  • Purpose: To educate developers on building agent harnesses and leveraging Jev models for efficient agent engineering. Sydney Runkle, Allie Laabs, and Hunter Lovell discuss building agent harnesses using Jev, a System One model from TypeSafe AI. They explore how Jev differs from traditional LLMs by providing fast, typed-safe, non-text-generating decision-making capabilities (Choice, Score, Noul) that make agent development faster and cheaper. Hunter Lovell demonstrates practical integration using LangChain, LangGraph, and LangSmith middleware for tool validation and model routing.

Topic Map

Introduction to Agent Engineering and LangSmith

  • Explanation: Sydney Runkle introduces the speakers and sets the context of the agent development lifecycle (build, test, deploy, monitor, govern).
  • Key claims:
    • Agents are a new kind of software with endless inputs and non-deterministic outputs.
    • LangSmith Fleet enables building agents without code.
  • Examples:
    • Preparing for tomorrow's meeting using integrated Slack, Gmail, and Google Docs apps.
  • Terminology:
    • LangSmith
    • Agent Development Lifecycle
    • LangGraph
    • DeepAgents
  • Why it matters: Establishes the platform context for engineering robust AI agents.

What is Jev and System One Models

  • Explanation: Allie Laabs explains Jev as a System One model from TypeSafe AI that does not generate text, but instead makes fast, type-safe decisions.
  • Key claims:
    • Jev does not generate text; it is a System One model focused on fast, type-safe decisions.
    • 200-200x faster and 40-400x cheaper than traditional LLMs for structured choices.
  • Examples:
    • Routing a support ticket to billing, technical, or sales.
  • Terminology:
    • System One
    • System Two
    • TypeSafe AI
    • LLM Gateway
  • Why it matters: Introduces a new class of models designed specifically for fast machine-to-machine decisions rather than heavy generative text.

The Three Types of Questions: Choice, Score, Noul

  • Explanation: Detailed breakdown of the interface types offered by Jev: Choice (classification), Score (scaling along an axis), and Noul (Bernoulli probability / boolean continuum).
  • Key claims:
    • Choice picks one option from a list.
    • Score rates the state on a scale from 0 to n.
    • Noul (Bernoulli probability) evaluates if a statement is true or false on a continuous 0 to 1 scale.
  • Examples:
    • Evaluating customer frustration levels on a scale.
    • Checking if a message conveys urgency or time-sensitivity.
  • Terminology:
    • Choice
    • Score
    • Noul
    • Bernoulli Probability
  • Why it matters: Provides developers with explicit structural primitives for decision-making.

Live Walkthrough: Implementing Jev in LangChain Harness

  • Explanation: Hunter Lovell demonstrates Python code using LangChain and Jev middleware for auto-mode tool validation and model routing.
  • Key claims:
    • Jev middleware can intercept tool calls and block destructive actions based on defined safety criteria.
    • Model router middleware uses Jev to select between fast and deep models based on prompt complexity.
  • Examples:
    • Blocking a permanent customer account deletion tool call when unauthorized.
    • Routing a prompt to a fast model vs deep model depending on task requirements.
  • Terminology:
    • AutoModeMiddleware
    • ModelRouterMiddleware
    • LangSmith Tracing
    • SupportState
  • Why it matters: Shows practical, production-ready code integration of Jev into existing LangChain agent architectures.

Key Points

Jev is API-first software

  • Explanation: Jev is not an end-user product; it is an API product meant to be integrated into software by programmers to build smart software.
  • Evidence: Hunter Lovell explains that Jev requires a programmer to put it into software.
  • Practical implication: Developers must write harness code around Jev to utilize its decision-making speed.

Bridging human interfaces and machine code

  • Explanation: Traditional tool calling uses text generation as a bridge between machine execution and human interfaces, which is inefficient.
  • Evidence: Hunter Lovell contrasts CLI tool calling with direct machine-to-machine decision-making.
  • Practical implication: Using Jev avoids unnecessary text generation overhead in backend logic.

Observability and Auditing

  • Explanation: LangSmith tracing provides full visibility into Jev decisions, probabilities, confidence scores, and middleware executions.
  • Evidence: Hunter Lovell demonstrates viewing traces in LangSmith for TypeSafeClassifier and ModelRouterMiddleware.
  • Practical implication: Developers can audit exactly why an agent took a specific path or why a tool call was blocked.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Agent Development Lifecycle

  • How it works: Iterative process of building, testing, deploying, and monitoring AI agents.
  • Components:
    • Build
    • Test
    • Deploy
    • Monitor
    • Govern
  • When to use: When engineering enterprise-grade AI agents systematically.

Jev Question Types

  • How it works: Categorizes input state evaluation into three distinct structured output types.
  • Components:
    • Choice
    • Score
    • Noul
  • When to use: When designing agent decision points, safety checks, or model routing.

Examples & Case Studies

A customer support agent attempts to delete a customer account without administrator approval.

  • Illustrates: AutoModeMiddleware blocking risky tool execution using Jev.
  • Lesson: Jev prevents unauthorized destructive actions by evaluating risk probability before tool execution.

A prompt is evaluated by ModelRouterMiddleware to choose between a fast model and a deep model.

  • Illustrates: Optimizing cost and latency by routing tasks appropriately.
  • Lesson: Simple tasks use fast models, while complex tasks use reasoning-heavy models.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Install LangChain TypeSafe integration for Python.
    • Implement AutoModeMiddleware for tool safety checks.
    • Use ModelRouterMiddleware to optimize model costs.
  • Strategic:
    • Adopt System One models for high-frequency decision points in agent loops.
    • Prioritize auditability and observability in agent harnesses using LangSmith.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do context length limits affect complex state evaluations?
    • What are the best practices for setting confidence thresholds in domain-specific tasks?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Jev is 200-200x faster and 40-400x cheaper than traditional LLMs. (Performance benchmark)

Notable Quotes

"Agents are a new kind of software. Endless inputs and non-deterministic outputs." (at 0:02) "Jev does not generate text. It is a System One model from TypeSafe AI."

Compressed Summary

  • Jev is a fast, type-safe System One model for structured agent decisions.
  • Supports three question types: Choice, Score, and Noul.
  • Integrates smoothly into LangChain via AutoMode and ModelRouter middleware.
  • LangSmith provides comprehensive tracing and observability for agent decisions.
  • Keywords: agent harness, jev, typesafe, langchain, middleware
  • Core insight: Building robust agent harnesses requires specialized System One models like Jev for fast, type-safe decision-making rather than relying solely on heavy generative LLMs.
